claims.text: A hybrid machine-learning interatomic-potential and iterative thermodynamic-integration workflow will significantly reduce the cost of calculating fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The hybrid workflow will retain fidelity in phase free energies and entropy contributions.
The ML interatomic potential will be trained on a sparse set of high-quality ab initio molecular-dynamics data.
The ML potential will rapidly explore the free-energy landscape.
Iterative thermodynamic integration will be supplemented by perturbative corrections for vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
A representative training set over the temperature range of interest is a condition for extension to multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The ML potential can serve as a surrogate force field for exploration and integration of the free-energy surfaces.
Explicit corrections can capture the relevant entropic and anharmonic effects omitted or approximated by the surrogate.
Using the ML energy landscape reduces the number of explicit ab initio calculations required.
Perturbatively corrected iterative integration accurately retains vibrational entropy and electron–vibration coupling.
The combined workflow will drastically reduce computational cost relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
For elemental and binary systems, the workflow will provide results comparable to TOR-TILD.
The workflow will provide an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational time relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
Calculated free energies will agree with TOR-TILD benchmarks within a few meV per atom.
Derived phase-boundary predictions will agree with TOR-TILD benchmarks within a few kelvin.
The workflow is expected to be effective for elemental, binary, and moderately complex multicomponent systems near their melting points.
Systems with highly nonlinear anharmonic effects may require additional calibration.
ML-augmented predictions differing by more than a few meV per atom in phase free energy or a few kelvin in melting temperature from the reference workflows would falsify the hypothesis.
